props.title: Meet Joe Black

sections.content: Meet Joe Black (1998) reimagines death as a curious explorer in human form, with Brad Pitt delivering an otherworldly performance as Death incarnate experiencing mortal life. The film builds on the 1934 classic Death Takes a Holiday, but director Martin Brest expands the concept into a sweeping meditation on mortality, love, and what makes life worth living. At nearly three hours, it's an unusually patient big-budget film that devotes substantial time to small moments - shared glances, quiet conversations, and the simple pleasure of peanut butter. Anthony Hopkins grounds the film as William Parrish, a media mogul facing his mortality with remarkable grace.

movies.slug: The original tale of Death taking human form to understand why mortals fear him

sections.content: The film's exploration of death through a romantic lens connects to other supernatural love stories like The Sixth Sense (1999) and City of Angels (1998), but takes a more contemplative approach. Rather than focusing on thriller elements or tragic romance, Meet Joe Black uses its supernatural premise to examine human relationships, particularly between fathers and daughters. The chemistry between Claire Forlani and Brad Pitt creates an unusual love triangle where Death himself learns about human connection. SUBHEAD: Visual and Thematic Sophistication

Cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki brings extraordinary visual poetry to ordinary moments, presaging his later work on The Tree of Life (2011). The film's infamous car accident scene remains one of cinema's most shocking transitions, but it's the intimate moments that showcase the technical mastery - candlelit dinners, sunrise conversations, and elaborate party sequences all carry subtle weight. Thomas Newman's score enhances these moments without overwhelming them, creating a dreamy atmosphere that supports the film's metaphysical elements.
